title: QBR / Unit cost review - $/1M output tokens trending up
next_steps: Redwood to export a 30-day breakdown of blended $/1M output tokens by model and region for HelioDesk (including cache hit rate and routing notes).
HelioDesk to share the timing/details of their routing change (model defaults + region preferences) and any prompt/template changes that may affect cacheability.
Redwood to run a quick analysis of cache hit-rate drop and propose specific prefix caching / prompt normalization steps.
Redwood to propose a dedicated capacity option for eu-west with a cost/latency comparison vs current hosted routing.
Follow-up working session: 45 minutes with HelioDesk infra team to review a draft “cost drivers” dashboard view and agree on guardrails.
content:
Fireflies.ai Notetaker
Meeting: QBR / Unit cost review - $/1M output tokens trending up
Date: 2025-02-12
Time: 5:00pm - 5:42pm PT
Duration: 42 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Marissa Cole, Logan Wright, Allison Grant
HelioDesk: Anika Patel, James O'Neil, Sofia Ramirez

Summary (auto-generated)
- HelioDesk escalated that blended cost per 1M output tokens has increased ~18–25% over the last 3 weeks.
- Redwood walked through likely drivers: region mix shift (more eu-west), model mix shift (more larger model usage), cache hit-rate degradation, and a small impact from runtime config changes.
- Agreed on concrete next steps: Redwood to provide breakdown exports and to recommend cache/prompt changes; HelioDesk to share routing/prompt changes and confirm requirements for cost reporting.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) What exactly increased (blended $/1M output tokens) and over what window
2) Region mix and failover events
3) Model mix changes and routing defaults
4) Cache hit-rate trends (prefix/KV)
5) Mitigations: caching, batching, quant profiles, dedicated capacity
6) Reporting + next QBR workflow

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood: send 30-day model/region/tier export + cache metrics (Owner: Marissa)
- Redwood: investigate cache hit-rate drop in eu-west route (Owner: Logan)
- HelioDesk: share routing policy + prompt template changes timeline (Owner: James)
- Redwood: share eu-west dedicated pricing ballpark + SLA notes (Owner: Marissa)

Questions (auto-generated)
- Does “blended” include credits/discounts or just compute?
- Is the increase concentrated in eu-west only or across regions?
- Did HelioDesk change prompt templates (affecting cache) or increase average output length?


Transcript

[00:00] Marissa Cole: Alright, cool. Hey everyone, thanks for making time. This is our QBR but I know the main agenda is the unit cost spike you all flagged—specifically the blended dollars per one million output tokens.

[00:10] Anika Patel: Yep. Thanks, Marissa. We’re seeing it in our internal reporting and, honestly, it’s starting to show up in our margins. So we want to understand what changed and what we can do.

[00:21] Sofia Ramirez: And just to level-set, finance is tracking it weekly now. We were steady-ish and then it jumped.

[00:29] Marissa Cole: Makes sense. Logan and Allison are on too—Logan owns telemetry/analytics on our side, Allison is SRE/observability. We’ll walk through drivers and then land on next steps.

[00:41] Logan Wright: Hi everyone.

[00:43] Allison Grant: Hey.

[00:46] James O'Neil: Hey.

[00:48] Marissa Cole: Before we jump in—Anika, when you say “unit cost,” are you using our invoice totals divided by output tokens? Or your own blended estimate?

[00:58] Sofia Ramirez: For now, it’s invoice line items for usage plus the credits we apply, divided by output tokens from your usage export. I know that’s not perfect.

[01:11] Marissa Cole: Got it. That’s close to how we think about “blended,” except internally we separate some overhead allocations and we also track pre-discount vs post-discount. For today, we’ll stick to what you’re feeling: effective $/1M output tokens.

[01:27] Anika Patel: The main thing is: did price change, did the model change, or did latency force us to re-route?

[01:35] Marissa Cole: Totally. Let’s anchor on the timeline. You said “last three weeks” in the email—do you have a date range?

[01:43] Sofia Ramirez: Starting around Jan 22nd. We saw about 18% up week over week, then another bump.

[01:52] Logan Wright: That lines up with what I see in our aggregates. There’s a noticeable shift around the 21st/22nd and then again around the 28th.

[02:03] James O'Neil: That’s… around when we changed some routing rules, I think. Not 100% sure.

[02:09] Marissa Cole: Okay, helpful. Let’s split drivers into buckets: mix shifts (region, model), then efficiency (cache, batching), then any platform changes.

[02:21] Logan Wright: I’ll share what we see. So: your eu-west share of output tokens increased from ~12% of your volume to ~31% over that period.

[02:33] Anika Patel: Wait, 31%? That seems high.

[02:36] James O'Neil: We did set eu-west as preferred for a bunch of customers because of data residency requirements. That might be it.

[02:44] Logan Wright: Yup, and eu-west unit costs are higher for the same model right now—GPU supply, and your route also had lower cache hit.

[02:54] Sofia Ramirez: So region mix alone explains what, like… all of it?

[02:59] Logan Wright: Not all, but a good chunk. Roughly speaking, holding model constant, eu-west is about 9–14% more expensive on blended compute per output token than us-east for the same settings, in your current usage pattern.

[03:15] Allison Grant: Also, there were a couple of short failover windows in late Jan where we pushed more traffic through a higher-cost pool to preserve latency SLOs. It wasn’t huge, but it shows up.

[03:26] James O'Neil: Is that on your side or ours?

[03:28] Allison Grant: On ours. We had capacity pressure in one of the clusters and routed to a compatible pool. We can point you to the incident notes, but it’s not like a multi-day thing.

[03:41] Marissa Cole: The bigger factor is probably model mix + cache. Logan, can you talk model?

[03:46] Logan Wright: Yeah. Second driver: your share of “large” model output tokens increased. Specifically, Llama-3-70B went from about 38% of your output tokens to about 57%.

[04:00] Anika Patel: We didn’t think we changed that much.

[04:03] James O'Neil: We rolled out a quality tweak for summarization and moved a chunk from the 8B to the 70B. That’s probably it.

[04:11] Marissa Cole: That’s consistent. Larger model + eu-west + less cacheable prompts is a perfect storm.

[04:20] Sofia Ramirez: Okay but—our product team says output quality is better, so maybe it’s worth it, but we need to control the spend.

[04:31] Marissa Cole: Right, so the question is: can we get the cost down while keeping quality? Usually we do that via (1) caching/prefix reuse, (2) routing “smart default” so 70B only when needed, (3) quantization profile where acceptable, and (4) dedicated capacity in the higher-cost region.

[04:52] Anika Patel: Let’s talk caching. We thought we were caching. We use your streaming API and the prompts are pretty templated.

[05:01] Logan Wright: You do have caching enabled, but the hit rate changed. In us-east, your prefix cache hit rate is around 22–24%. In eu-west, it fell to ~9–11% over the same period.

[05:15] James O'Neil: That’s weird. Why would eu-west be worse?

[05:19] Logan Wright: Two common reasons: (1) traffic is more “bursty” and your requests don’t stick to the same cache footprint; (2) prompt template drift—tiny differences like timestamps, request ids, or user-specific preamble in the first N tokens kills prefix matching.

[05:37] Anika Patel: We did add some dynamic policy text at the top. Like, a compliance banner.

[05:43] Logan Wright: That can do it, yeah.

[05:45] Marissa Cole: Also, if eu-west traffic is split across more routes/pools, cache gets fragmented. We can check whether you’re hitting multiple runtime_config variants.

[05:56] James O'Neil: We do multi-region with fallback. But we thought the cache was global.

[06:01] Logan Wright: It’s not global across regions. It’s per region/pool, for data locality and latency. So if you moved a third of traffic to eu-west, it basically started cold.

[06:14] Sofia Ramirez: So the “cache savings” we had in us-east didn’t carry.

[06:18] Logan Wright: Exactly.

[06:20] Anika Patel: Can we warm it? Or do anything to make it better quickly?

[06:24] Logan Wright: The fastest win is prompt normalization: make sure the first ~200-400 tokens are identical for repeated workflows. Put dynamic stuff later, or move it into a tool call argument, or compress it into a stable token.

[06:41] Marissa Cole: Another option: if the compliance banner is required, we can help you restructure it so the static part is first and only a short variable segment changes.

[06:52] James O'Neil: Okay. That’s actionable.

[06:55] Allison Grant: And from the platform side, we can confirm whether eu-west is splitting you across different pools because of autoscaling. If so, we can pin you to fewer pools or talk about dedicated.

[07:09] Anika Patel: Let’s park dedicated for a sec. I want to understand if there were any changes on your end that made it worse besides region.

[07:17] Allison Grant: There was one runtime rollout in late Jan—mostly kernel selection updates for certain sequence lengths. It improved p95 latency for most, but unit cost should be neutral or slightly better. I don’t see a regression there.

[07:33] Logan Wright: +1. The cost increase correlates way more strongly to mix + cache than to any internal release.

[07:40] Sofia Ramirez: When you say “mix,” can you quantify “how much is region vs model vs cache”? Like a decomposition?

[07:48] Marissa Cole: We can. Internally we’re building an explain panel for exactly this—driver attribution like region mix shift, model mix shift, cache hit-rate effects. For now, we can do a manual breakdown for your account.

[08:03] James O'Neil: That would help. Because right now it’s just “it went up,” and we’re guessing.

[08:09] Marissa Cole: Totally. Rough estimate from what Logan pulled: of the ~20% effective $/1M increase, about ~8–10 points is region mix shift, ~6–8 points is model mix shift, and ~3–5 points is cache hit-rate dropping (plus a little noise from failover and output length).

[08:29] Anika Patel: Output length changed too?

[08:32] Logan Wright: Slightly. Your average output tokens per request increased ~7% on the summarization route. If you’re paying per output token, that should scale linearly, but the efficiency impacts can change if longer generations reduce batching efficiency.

[08:49] James O'Neil: We did raise max tokens for a feature.

[08:52] Marissa Cole: Okay.

[08:54] Anika Patel: What about batching? We didn’t change anything. Is Redwood doing continuous batching automatically?

[09:00] Logan Wright: Yes, but the realized batching depends on concurrency and latency targets. If your traffic in eu-west is spiky and you also set lower latency timeouts, batch sizes shrink.

[09:14] Allison Grant: Also if you moved a segment of users to eu-west, concurrency per pool may be lower than us-east, so the batcher has less to work with.

[09:26] Sofia Ramirez: So, to lower cost in eu-west, we’d want… more consistent traffic? That’s hard.

[09:33] Marissa Cole: Not necessarily consistent traffic, but we can: (1) consolidate routes, (2) increase allowable batching window slightly on non-interactive flows, (3) improve caching so fewer tokens hit GPU in the first place, and (4) consider reserved capacity if eu-west is now a big chunk.

[09:53] James O'Neil: Can we do something like “70B only for hard cases”? We don’t have a classifier.

[09:59] Marissa Cole: Yes. A common pattern is two-pass: try the smaller model, and only escalate if it fails a cheap heuristic. Or use a reranker/eval signal. We can help design that.

[10:12] Anika Patel: We also worry about quality regressions if we swap models.

[10:16] Marissa Cole: Understood. We can set up a canary routing policy so only a percentage uses the smaller model. And we can track quality with your eval set if you have one.

[10:26] James O'Neil: We have a small golden set.

[10:28] Logan Wright: Nice.

[10:30] Sofia Ramirez: I’m going to ask a finance question: could discounts or credits have changed? Like, did our effective rate go up because credits ran out?

[10:39] Marissa Cole: Good question. I don’t manage credits directly but we can check. From what I can see, your contracted discounts didn’t change in that window. The change is mostly usage behavior.

[10:52] Sofia Ramirez: Okay.

[10:54] Anika Patel: Let’s get specific. What data can you send us that is “source of truth”? We need it weekly.

[11:01] Marissa Cole: We can send a CSV export for the last 30 days with daily rows: blended $/1M output tokens, output tokens, and then dimensions: model, region, and your tier. We’ll also include cache hit rate and an estimated cache savings field.

[11:19] Logan Wright: And we can add a “runtime_config” tag so you can see if you’re split across variants. That helps pinpoint fragmentation.

[11:27] James O'Neil: That would be great.

[11:29] Allison Grant: And we can include a note for any days with abnormal failover/routing so you can annotate.

[11:35] Sofia Ramirez: Perfect.

[11:38] Anika Patel: On caching, what do you need from us to diagnose? Prompt samples?

[11:43] Logan Wright: If you can share two or three representative prompt templates (redacted), and also confirm if you include request IDs or timestamps early in the prompt.

[11:54] James O'Neil: We do include a conversation id near the top.

[11:58] Logan Wright: That’s likely hurting.

[12:00] Anika Patel: But we thought the model needs it.

[12:02] Logan Wright: The model doesn’t need it in the first tokens. You can move it later, or pass it as metadata not included in the prompt.

[12:11] Marissa Cole: If you’re using tool/function calling, you can keep identifiers in the tool args rather than in the system prompt.

[12:18] James O'Neil: We’re using tool calling, yes.

[12:20] Marissa Cole: Then you have an easy out.

[12:23] Sofia Ramirez: How quickly would we see savings if we fix prompt normalization?

[12:27] Logan Wright: Pretty quickly—within a day or two, depending on traffic. Cache warms as requests repeat.

[12:34] Allison Grant: Assuming you aren’t constantly shifting regions, yes.

[12:38] Anika Patel: Let’s talk dedicated, because we might be in eu-west for good now.

[12:44] Marissa Cole: Sure. Dedicated would give you more predictable throughput and can help cost if your sustained usage is high—also you get more stable cache behavior since you’re pinned to a pool.

[12:57] Sofia Ramirez: Is it cheaper than hosted?

[13:00] Marissa Cole: It depends. If you have steady utilization, dedicated can be cheaper per token. If utilization is spiky, hosted is often better. But dedicated in eu-west can also protect you from the “premium” pricing swings we have when capacity is tight.

[13:18] James O'Neil: We do have diurnal patterns. Weekdays are heavy.

[13:22] Marissa Cole: Then we can model it. We can give you a comparison: current hosted effective $/1M vs a reserved pool sized to your p50/p90, plus burst.

[13:33] Anika Patel: We’d need at least an estimate. Procurement takes time.

[13:38] Marissa Cole: Understood. I can send a ballpark with assumptions and then loop in our commercial team if you want to go deeper.

[13:46] Sofia Ramirez: Please do.

[13:48] Marissa Cole: Cool.

[13:50] Anika Patel: Also, we sometimes compare to OpenAI. Their cost looks stable. So we need to justify why this moved.

[13:58] Marissa Cole: Makes sense. The big difference is: if you changed region residency and model size, any provider would see changes. But Redwood gives you more knobs—and we’ll help you implement them.

[14:11] James O'Neil: Can you confirm your “blended cost” includes overhead? Like control plane.

[14:16] Logan Wright: Internally yes, we allocate overhead for our own reporting. For customer billing, you’re paying per token on hosted. For the export we send, we’ll keep it aligned with the billed usage so it ties out.

[14:29] Sofia Ramirez: Great, tie-out is important.

[14:32] Allison Grant: Also, note the invoice vs near-real-time dashboard can differ for a day or two if there are late metering events. But for a 30-day lookback, it should reconcile.

[14:44] Anika Patel: We did notice some day-to-day variance that didn’t match. That might be the late events.

[14:50] Logan Wright: Possibly. We’ll call it out in the export.

[14:54] Marissa Cole: Okay. Let’s align on what you need from us as “root cause.” My view: (1) you moved more traffic into eu-west; (2) you increased 70B usage; (3) prompt changes reduced cache hit-rate in eu-west; (4) a couple of small platform routing events, minor.

[15:11] Anika Patel: That sounds right.

[15:13] James O'Neil: I want to validate point 3. If we fix prompts and cache hit-rate goes back to 20% in eu-west, how much does that save?

[15:22] Logan Wright: Roughly, going from 10% to 20% prefix hit rate on your workload is about 4–6% reduction in effective compute per output token. The exact depends on how much of your prompt is reused.

[15:38] James O'Neil: Okay.

[15:39] Sofia Ramirez: So it won’t fully offset the region move.

[15:42] Marissa Cole: Correct, but combined with smarter model routing, you can claw back a lot.

[15:49] Anika Patel: For model routing, what’s the simplest step?

[15:53] Marissa Cole: Identify one route where 70B is overkill—maybe internal summarization or categorization—and test moving 20% back to the smaller model. If quality holds, expand.

[16:05] James O'Neil: We can do that.

[16:07] Anika Patel: Is there a quantization profile we should use? We heard you have that.

[16:12] Logan Wright: Yes, we have quantization profiles, but they have quality tradeoffs. For Llama-3-70B, we can try an 8-bit-ish profile first (the naming is a bit confusing) and validate on your golden set.

[16:27] Marissa Cole: We’ll recommend a profile and how to slice cost by it. But I don’t want to push quant if quality is sensitive.

[16:35] Anika Patel: We can test it.

[16:37] Allison Grant: From SRE side, quant profiles can also change latency variability. We’ll watch p95.

[16:44] James O'Neil: Okay.

[16:46] Marissa Cole: Sofia, for weekly reporting—do you want an email summary, or do you want us to give you access to a dashboard view?

[16:54] Sofia Ramirez: Email is fine for now, but longer term dashboard access would be great.

[17:00] Marissa Cole: Internally we’re building a unit economics dashboard. It’s not customer-facing, but we can use it to generate consistent exports. We can also do a standing monthly review.

[17:12] Anika Patel: That’s good.

[17:14] James O'Neil: Also, are there any knobs we can set to avoid expensive failovers? Like, prefer cost over latency?

[17:22] Allison Grant: We do have routing policies that can bias for cost vs latency, but we’re careful because it can violate your SLA expectations. For your non-interactive jobs, we can route to a cheaper pool with a higher queue tolerance.

[17:39] James O'Neil: That would help for batch jobs.

[17:41] Marissa Cole: Great point. We’ll separate interactive vs batch routes.

[17:47] Anika Patel: On the eu-west move, we did it for compliance. But not all users need it. Could we keep some in us-east?

[17:55] James O'Neil: We can. We just defaulted to eu-west.

[17:58] Marissa Cole: If you can segment, that’s the cleanest cost lever: keep latency-sensitive and non-residency traffic in the cheaper region.

[18:09] Sofia Ramirez: That would probably be easiest for finance too. Residency users cost more, others less.

[18:16] Logan Wright: And then caching improves as each segment stabilizes in its region.

[18:21] Anika Patel: Okay.

[18:23] Marissa Cole: Let’s confirm next steps and owners.

[18:27] Marissa Cole: First, Redwood will send a 30-day breakdown: daily blended $/1M output tokens, output tokens, by model and region, include cache hit-rate and estimated savings. I’ll own that; Logan will provide the data.

[18:43] Logan Wright: Yes.

[18:44] Marissa Cole: Second, James—you’ll share the routing policy change timeline and prompt template changes around Jan 20–28.

[18:52] James O'Neil: Yep, I can send a doc or just bullet points.

[18:55] Marissa Cole: Bullet points are fine.

[18:57] Marissa Cole: Third, Logan will look specifically at eu-west cache fragmentation and whether you’re split across runtime configs.

[19:05] Logan Wright: Yup.

[19:06] Marissa Cole: Fourth, I’ll send a dedicated eu-west ballpark with assumptions—maybe by end of week.

[19:13] Sofia Ramirez: That works.

[19:14] Marissa Cole: Fifth, we’ll schedule a working session—45 minutes—next week, to go through the breakdown and decide: prompt normalization changes, model routing experiment, and whether we pilot quant profile.

[19:28] Anika Patel: Sounds good.

[19:30] James O'Neil: Can we also get guidance on prompt normalization best practices? Like a short checklist.

[19:35] Logan Wright: Yes, we can include that.

[19:38] Allison Grant: And I’ll add any notes on days with abnormal routing so you don’t chase ghosts.

[19:44] Anika Patel: Great.

[19:46] Sofia Ramirez: One last thing: the question from leadership is, “is Redwood becoming more expensive?” What do we say?

[19:54] Marissa Cole: The truthful message is: your effective cost moved because usage mix shifted—more eu-west, more large model, lower cache hit. Our underlying pricing didn’t change. And we have levers to bring it back down.

[20:10] Anika Patel: Okay.

[20:12] James O'Neil: Works.

[20:14] Marissa Cole: Cool. Anything else before we drop?

[20:18] Anika Patel: No, this was helpful.

[20:20] Sofia Ramirez: Thanks.

[20:22] James O'Neil: Thanks everyone.

[20:24] Allison Grant: Thanks.

[20:25] Logan Wright: Thank you.

[20:27] Marissa Cole: Alright, I’ll send the follow-up email with the export and proposed times.

(End of transcript excerpt — Fireflies transcription ended early; call continued briefly for scheduling)
